sections.body:
The supply chain disruptions of the pandemic era revealed Pakistan's structural vulnerability to external shocks while simultaneously creating potential opportunities. As global companies sought to diversify their supply chains away from excessive dependence on single-country sources—particularly China—Pakistan had an opportunity to attract relocated or diversified production capacity.

However, capturing this opportunity required Pakistan to address longstanding competitive weaknesses: high energy costs, unreliable electricity supply, burdensome regulatory frameworks, inadequate logistics infrastructure, and skill gaps in the workforce. The countries that successfully attracted supply chain relocation—Vietnam, Bangladesh, and others—had developed competitive advantages in these areas over years of sustained policy attention.

sections.title: Building Supply Chain Resilience
sections.body:
Pakistan's approach to building supply chain resilience must operate on multiple levels. At the firm level, businesses can develop more diverse supplier relationships, maintain larger buffer inventories of critical inputs, and invest in process flexibility. At the sector level, industry associations can coordinate to develop alternative sourcing strategies and advocate for policy support.

At the national level, policies that develop domestic capabilities in key input industries reduce import dependence. Improving logistics infrastructure—ports, roads, warehousing, and digital trade facilitation—reduces the impact of external disruptions on domestic production. Trade agreements that provide alternative market access and supply sources enhance resilience.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Global supply chain disruptions have revealed the vulnerability embedded in Pakistan's industrial integration into global networks. The country's textile and manufacturing sectors, while benefiting enormously from global integration in normal times, face severe stress when those networks are disrupted by pandemics, geopolitical conflicts, or natural disasters. Building resilience requires both firm-level adaptations and national policy reforms that address structural weaknesses—ensuring that Pakistan can maintain production and protect livelihoods even when global supply networks are under strain.

publications.title: Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Rising Costs, Shrinking Wallets. An analysis of how global inflationary pressures translate into a domestic crisis in Pakistan.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan/Global Inflation Wave and Its Impact on Pakistan.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The world economy is experiencing a significant inflationary wave, with major economies like the United States and the European Union grappling with rising prices across virtually every sector. This global phenomenon is not confined to the borders of advanced economies—it ripples outward, touching developing nations like Pakistan with particularly harsh consequences. For a country already struggling with fiscal imbalances and a fragile economic structure, external inflationary pressures can quickly translate into a crisis of daily survival for millions of citizens.

sections.title: How Global Inflation Reaches Pakistan
sections.body:
Pakistan is a net importer of several essential commodities, including petroleum products, edible oils, industrial raw materials, and machinery. When inflation rises in major economies, the cost of producing and exporting these goods increases. This means Pakistan pays more for the same volume of imports, effectively importing inflation from abroad.

Additionally, the US Dollar's dominant role in global trade means that when the dollar strengthens—as it often does during inflationary periods driven by monetary tightening—Pakistan's rupee buys less in the international market. The result is a compounding effect: higher global prices combined with a weaker domestic currency create a double burden on the Pakistani economy.

sections.title: Impact on Fuel, Food, and Raw Materials
sections.body:
Three sectors feel the impact most acutely. First, fuel: Pakistan is heavily dependent on imported oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG). As global energy prices surge—driven by geopolitical tensions, OPEC decisions, and post-pandemic demand rebounds—Pakistan's energy import bill skyrockets. This makes electricity generation, transportation, and industrial production more expensive, cascading into higher prices across the entire economy.

Second, food prices: global food inflation, partly driven by supply chain disruptions, climate events, and conflict zones, raises the cost of imported edible oils, wheat, and pulses. For a country where food constitutes a large portion of household budgets, this directly diminishes the purchasing power of ordinary Pakistanis.

Third, raw materials: industries ranging from textiles to chemicals depend on imported inputs. When these become expensive, production costs rise, leading to either higher prices for consumers or reduced output—neither of which is desirable.

sections.title: The Human Cost
sections.body: The most direct consequence of imported inflation is felt by low- and middle-income households. As prices of everyday essentials—flour, cooking oil, electricity, fuel—climb relentlessly, families find themselves spending a larger fraction of their income just to maintain basic living standards. Savings shrink, debt increases, and poverty rates rise. Pakistan's already stretched social safety nets come under enormous pressure, often proving inadequate to cushion the most vulnerable segments of society.

sections.title: Policy Responses and Their Limitations
sections.body:
The Pakistani government and the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) have attempted to manage inflationary pressures through a combination of monetary tightening, subsidies, and import controls. Raising interest rates, for example, can reduce domestic demand and cool inflation but also stifles economic growth and raises the cost of borrowing for businesses and individuals alike.

Subsidies on fuel and food can provide short-term relief but are fiscally unsustainable, especially for a country with limited revenue and a heavy debt burden. Import restrictions may protect foreign exchange reserves in the short run but can lead to shortages and black markets.

Ultimately, Pakistan's capacity to insulate itself from global inflationary waves is constrained by structural vulnerabilities: a narrow export base, low foreign exchange reserves, high import dependence, and limited fiscal space. Addressing these structural issues is essential for building resilience against future inflationary shocks.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: The global inflation wave is a sobering reminder of how interconnected today's economies are. For Pakistan, rising international prices translate directly into hardship for its citizens, straining household budgets and government finances alike. While short-term policy measures can offer some relief, the deeper solution lies in structural reforms that reduce import dependence, boost exports, enhance productivity, and build fiscal buffers. Until such reforms take root, Pakistan will remain acutely vulnerable to the economic tides that originate far beyond its borders.

publications.title: Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: How the World's Reserve Currency Shapes Pakistan's Economy. Investigating the impact of a strong US Dollar on the Pakistani Rupee.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance/Currency Depreciation and the Dollar Dominance.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The US dollar's role as the world's dominant reserve currency and primary medium of international trade creates a structural asymmetry in the global economy. Countries that earn and hold reserves in dollars benefit from its stability and universal acceptance. Countries like Pakistan that must buy dollars to pay for essential imports and service dollar-denominated debt face a fundamental vulnerability: their economic well-being is significantly influenced by the value of a currency they do not control and a monetary policy set for American domestic conditions.

sections.title: The Mechanics of Rupee Depreciation
sections.body:
The Pakistani rupee's value is determined in foreign exchange markets by the supply and demand for rupees relative to other currencies, particularly the dollar. Several factors create persistent downward pressure on the rupee.

Pakistan's structural trade deficit—importing significantly more than it exports—means that the economy continuously demands more dollars than it earns from exports. This excess demand for dollars creates inherent depreciation pressure. When this deficit is not offset by sufficient inflows of foreign investment, remittances, or borrowing, reserves deplete and the rupee falls.

When the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates, the dollar strengthens globally as international capital flows toward higher-yielding dollar assets. This dollar appreciation is simultaneously rupee depreciation—the mirror image of dollar strength. Thus, American monetary policy decisions intended to address US domestic inflation directly affect Pakistan's exchange rate.

sections.title: The Import Cost Amplification
sections.body:
Currency depreciation creates an immediate and painful amplification of import costs. If Pakistan imports a barrel of oil at $80, and the rupee has depreciated by 20% over a year, the rupee cost of that same barrel has increased by 20%—even if the dollar price of oil remained unchanged.

This mechanism means that Pakistan effectively faces a double burden during periods of global stress: international commodity prices often rise at the same time that the rupee falls, as both are driven by dollar strengthening and global risk aversion. The combination of higher dollar prices and a weaker rupee can dramatically increase the rupee cost of essential imports within a short period, generating intense inflationary pressure.

sections.title: Impact on Businesses and Consumers
sections.body:
The business community faces multiple challenges from currency depreciation. Importers see their costs rise immediately when the rupee depreciates. Manufacturers who use imported raw materials face rising input costs, which they must either absorb—reducing profit margins—or pass on to consumers, contributing to inflation.

Exporters benefit from rupee depreciation in theory, as their goods become cheaper in international markets in dollar terms. However, if their production costs rise due to imported inputs and higher energy costs (themselves partly driven by import costs), the competitive gain is offset. The net benefit to exporters depends on their specific cost structure and the degree to which they can expand production at lower cost in dollar terms.

For consumers, currency depreciation is experienced as higher prices across virtually the entire basket of goods and services. From fuel prices at petrol stations to the cost of electronics, medicines, and processed foods—the depreciated rupee makes everything more expensive.

sections.title: The Political Economy of Exchange Rate Management
sections.body:
Managing the exchange rate involves difficult political choices. Artificially maintaining an overvalued exchange rate by intervening in currency markets to support the rupee can provide temporary relief from import cost increases but depletes foreign exchange reserves and creates distortions that ultimately require more painful correction.

Allowing market-determined exchange rate adjustments as required under IMF programs is often more economically rational but politically contentious given its immediate inflationary impact. Pakistani governments have historically alternated between periods of exchange rate suppression and sharp devaluations, each creating its own set of economic distortions and hardships.

sections.title: Reducing Dollar Vulnerability
sections.body:
Pakistan's long-term vulnerability to dollar dominance can be reduced through several strategies. Building export capacity across diverse sectors generates more dollar earnings domestically, reducing net import demand. Developing domestic production of currently imported goods reduces the dollar demand created by imports.

Diversifying trade and financing relationships—including increasing use of local currencies in bilateral trade with neighboring countries like China and the Gulf states—reduces, at the margin, the exclusive dominance of the dollar in Pakistan's international transactions. Building adequate foreign exchange reserves provides a buffer against short-term pressure without requiring immediate adjustment.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: The dollar's dominance in global trade and finance creates a structural challenge for Pakistan that cannot be resolved through exchange rate policy alone. Currency depreciation is both a symptom of underlying economic imbalances and a cause of further inflation and financial stress. Addressing Pakistan's currency vulnerability requires the hard work of structural economic transformation—building exports, reducing import dependence, improving fiscal discipline, and creating the conditions for stable, growth-enabling investment flows.

publications.title: Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Living on the Front Lines of a Global Crisis. How international climate agreements are shaping Pakistan's economic landscape.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy/Climate Change, Global Policies, and Pakistan's Economy.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: Pakistan stands at a painful paradox in the global climate crisis. Despite contributing less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, the country ranks consistently among the world's most vulnerable nations to the physical impacts of climate change. Extreme heat waves, devastating floods, glacial lake outburst floods, drought, and crop failures are no longer theoretical future scenarios—they are lived realities that are already reshaping Pakistan's economy and threatening its development trajectory.

sections.title: The Physical Reality of Climate Impacts
sections.body:
Pakistan's geographical position makes it acutely sensitive to climate variability. The 2022 super-floods—described by scientists as made significantly more likely and severe by climate change—provide the starkest illustration. These floods inundated approximately one-third of the country's land mass, killed over 1,700 people, displaced millions, destroyed critical infrastructure, and caused economic losses estimated at over $30 billion.

Agricultural losses during the 2022 floods were catastrophic: millions of acres of crops destroyed, vast livestock herds lost, and irrigation infrastructure damaged. In a country where agriculture employs approximately 40% of the workforce and contributes around 20% of GDP, such losses have profound ripple effects throughout the economy. Reduced agricultural output drives food price inflation, reduces rural incomes, and increases food import requirements—all adding pressure to an already strained economy.

sections.title: Recurring Climate Shocks and Economic Stability
sections.body:
The 2022 floods were an extreme event but not an isolated one. Pakistan has experienced increasingly frequent and severe climate-related disruptions: intense heat waves that reduce agricultural productivity and worker output, irregular monsoons that affect crop planting and yields, glacial melting that threatens the long-term water security of the Indus Basin, and coastal erosion threatening populated areas in Sindh and Balochistan.

These recurring shocks create an environment of economic uncertainty that discourages investment, disrupts planning, and imposes continuous repair and recovery costs on a country with already limited fiscal resources. The cumulative economic cost of climate impacts—even without considering catastrophic events like the 2022 floods—represents a significant drag on Pakistan's development potential.

sections.title: International Climate Finance and Pakistan
sections.body:
The global discussion on climate finance has created both opportunities and frustrations for Pakistan. Developed countries have pledged billions in climate finance to help developing nations adapt to climate change and transition to cleaner energy—but the delivery of these commitments has been inconsistent and often falls short of pledged amounts.

Following the 2022 floods, Pakistan's advocacy for climate justice and loss-and-damage compensation drew international attention and contributed to the establishment of a Loss and Damage Fund at COP27. Accessing and effectively utilizing climate finance requires Pakistan to develop strong project pipelines, transparent financial management systems, and institutional capacity to negotiate with international climate funds.

sections.title: Global Climate Policies and Pakistan's Exports
sections.body:
Beyond direct physical impacts, global climate policies create important economic implications for Pakistan. The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM)—which imposes carbon costs on imports from countries without equivalent carbon pricing—threatens to raise the cost of Pakistani exports entering the EU market over time.

Pakistan's export-oriented industries, particularly textiles and leather, will face pressure to document and reduce their carbon footprints to maintain market access in climate-conscious importing countries. This creates both a compliance cost and an investment opportunity—firms that successfully transition to cleaner production processes may gain competitive advantages in premium export markets that reward sustainability credentials.

sections.title: Building Climate Resilience
sections.body:
Pakistan's national climate strategy must address both adaptation—reducing vulnerability to impacts that are already locked in—and mitigation—reducing emissions as part of the global effort to limit future warming. Adaptation priorities include flood protection infrastructure, drought-resistant crop varieties, efficient irrigation systems, early warning systems, and climate-resilient construction standards.

Mitigation involves transitioning Pakistan's energy sector toward renewables, improving energy efficiency, developing sustainable transportation, and protecting forests. Many of these investments have co-benefits for economic development—renewable energy reduces fuel import bills, efficient irrigation improves agricultural productivity, and forest protection supports rural livelihoods.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: Climate change represents an existential economic threat for Pakistan—one that is already manifesting in devastating floods, disrupted agriculture, and increased reliance on international emergency assistance. Pakistan's experience challenges the international community to deliver meaningful climate finance and ambitious emission reductions. Domestically, building climate resilience requires sustained investment, institutional development, and policy coherence across economic sectors. The cost of inaction—measured in recurring disasters, agricultural decline, and development setbacks—far exceeds the investment required for adaptation and mitigation.

publications.title: China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Promises, Progress, and Shifting Priorities. An analysis of CPEC's trajectory amidst shifting global economic dynamics.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy/China-Pakistan Economic Corridor in a Changing Global Economy.png

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) was launched with enormous ambition—a flagship project of China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) that promised to transform Pakistan's infrastructure, energy sector, and economic connectivity while cementing a strategic partnership between the two neighboring nations. A decade into implementation, CPEC has delivered significant results in certain areas while facing challenges from Pakistan's economic difficulties, changing global dynamics, and shifts in China's own economic priorities.

sections.title: CPEC's Foundational Vision
sections.body:
At its core, CPEC envisions connecting China's landlocked western Xinjiang region to the Arabian Sea through Pakistan's Gwadar port, creating a shorter and more economical route for Chinese trade and energy imports from the Middle East and Africa. For Pakistan, the corridor was meant to address two critical bottlenecks: an acute energy shortage crippling industrial production and an inadequate transportation network limiting economic activity.

The $62 billion investment—though revised figures vary—was structured to deliver energy projects, road and rail upgrades, and special economic zones (SEZs) that would attract industrial investment and create employment. The vision was of a Pakistan transformed into a regional hub of trade and manufacturing.

sections.title: Progress and Achievements
sections.body:
CPEC has delivered tangible results in Pakistan's power sector. Numerous energy projects—coal, solar, and hydropower—have been completed or are operational, adding significant capacity to the national grid. This has reduced, though not eliminated, Pakistan's chronic electricity shortages that had long suppressed industrial output.

Infrastructure investments have improved road connectivity in various corridors, and Gwadar port has seen significant development. These investments have created employment during construction and improved logistics in certain regions. For Pakistan, attracting such large-scale foreign investment at concessional terms was an achievement in itself given the country's challenging business environment.

sections.title: Challenges and Controversies
sections.body:
CPEC has also generated significant controversy and faces serious challenges. Critics have raised concerns about the transparency of contracts, the terms of financing, and the extent to which Pakistani businesses benefit from CPEC projects—noting that many contracts were awarded to Chinese firms with limited local participation.

The debt obligations associated with CPEC projects—including principal repayments and repatriated profits from independent power producers—have contributed to Pakistan's external financial pressures. The promised industrial cooperation through SEZs has been slower to materialize than anticipated, limiting the employment generation and technology transfer that were central to CPEC's developmental promises.

Geopolitical tensions in the region, security challenges—particularly in Balochistan, and inconsistent policy support from successive Pakistani governments have all slowed implementation.

sections.title: China's Changing Economic Priorities
sections.body:
China's own economic situation is evolving in ways that affect CPEC's trajectory. China's growth has moderated from its earlier double-digit rates, and the country is navigating significant internal economic transitions. The BRI overall has faced scrutiny over debt sustainability concerns, and China has become more selective and cautious in its overseas infrastructure investments.

This shift in Chinese priorities, combined with Pakistan's financial difficulties limiting its ability to fulfill obligations and attract complementary investments, means that CPEC's second phase focusing on industrial development has progressed more slowly than initially envisioned. Both countries need to recalibrate expectations and focus on ensuring that existing investments deliver their intended benefits before committing to ambitious new phases.

sections.title: The Path Forward
sections.body:
For CPEC to fulfill its transformative potential, several conditions are necessary. Pakistan must improve its business environment through regulatory reforms, consistent policy frameworks, and enhanced security—making SEZs genuinely attractive to both Chinese and international investors. Renegotiating the terms of existing energy agreements to reduce their fiscal burden on Pakistan would improve the corridor's overall economic sustainability.

Diversifying CPEC's scope to include more agriculture, technology, and services cooperation alongside physical infrastructure would better leverage Pakistan's comparative advantages. Greater transparency in project contracts and more meaningful participation of Pakistani firms would also address legitimate concerns about the distribution of benefits.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.body: CPEC remains a vital component of Pakistan's development strategy and a cornerstone of its strategic relationship with China. Despite falling short of its most ambitious initial projections, the corridor has delivered real infrastructure improvements and energy capacity. In a changing global economy where great power competition intensifies and China recalibrates its overseas investments, Pakistan must be a proactive and strategic partner—ensuring that CPEC delivers lasting economic benefits rather than merely creating debt obligations and foreign-dominated enclaves.

publications.title: Introduction to Monetary Economics
publications.author: Atiq Ur Rehman, Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Monetary Economics, 1st Edition. This book will be of interest to teachers and students of monetary economics, money and banking, macroeconomics and monetary policy.

sections.title: Major Features of this Edition
sections.body:
• Moderated Stylized facts on money demand and supply, and the relationships between monetary policy, inflation, output and unemployment in the economy.
  • Theories on money demand and supply, including precautionary and buffer stock models, and monetary aggregation.
  • Competing macroeconomic models of the Classical and Keynesian paradigms, along with a discussion of their validity and consistency with the stylized facts.
  • Excellent pedagogical features such as introductions, key concepts, end-of-chapter summaries, and review and discussion questions.

sections.title: About the Authors
sections.body:
Dr. Atiq ur Rehman is Associate Professor of Economics at University of Azad Jammu and Kashmir, UAJK and has taught monetary economics and macroeconomics for over 15 years.

Dr. Shakeel Shahzad is Assistant Professor of Economics at Bahria University, Islamabad and has taught monetary economics, macroeconomics, and econometrics for over 10 years.

publications.title: Corporate Governance and Profitability of Insurance Companies: Empirical Insights from Pakistan
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: An empirical investigation evaluating the impact of corporate governance structures—including board size, board independence, audit committee independence, and ownership concentration—on the profitability and financial performance of insurance companies in Pakistan.

sections.title: Journal & Publication Details
sections.body:
Journal: Pakistan Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences (PJHSS)
Volume/Issue: Vol. 11, No. 4 (2023)
DOI: 10.52131/pjhss.2023.1104.0716

sections.title: Abstract & Findings
sections.body: This empirical study analyzes the role of corporate governance mechanisms in influencing the financial performance and profitability of insurance firms operating in Pakistan. Using multi-year firm-level data, the paper examines key governance indicators including board size, board independence, audit committee oversight, and ownership concentration, measuring their relationship with Return on Assets (ROA) and Return on Equity (ROE). The findings provide strategic recommendations for regulatory bodies and financial sector leaders to enhance oversight, strengthen investor confidence, and ensure long-term stability in the insurance industry.

publications.title: Critical Discourse Analysis of Trauma Bonding in Female Victims of Intimate Partner Abuse: A Phenomenological Constructivist Approach
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: A phenomenological constructivist study applying Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) to deconstruct media labels, societal ideals, and cognitive dynamics that reinforce trauma bonding in female victims of intimate partner abuse.

sections.title: Journal & Publication Details
sections.body:
Journal: Sustainable Business and Society in Emerging Economies
Volume/Issue: Vol. 4, No. 4 (2022)
DOI: 10.26710/sbsee.v4i4.2496

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: Intimate partner abuse (IPA) is a socially prevalent issue across cultures. Despite the establishment of survivor institutes and anti-domestic violence NGOs, the voices of battered women have frequently failed to reach legal and governmental policy frameworks. Recent research indicates that women often remain bound to dangerously abusive relationships due to complex psychological and social factors. This study adopts a socio-cognitive approach and phenomenological constructivism to critically deconstruct media labels, societal expectations, and victim narratives. The findings show how these intersecting factors generate trauma bonding, forcing victims to stay in abusive environments, and highlighting the need for policy interventions tailored to survivor cognitive reality.

publications.title: Opening of Kartarpur Corridor: A Critical Discourse Analysis that How Indo-Pak Media Projected the Corridor Initiative
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: A Critical Discourse Analysis comparing how Pakistani and Indian media outlets projected the historic opening of the Kartarpur Corridor, contrasting narratives of peace and religious diplomacy with security concerns.

sections.title: Journal & Publication Details
sections.body:
Journal: Review of Politics and Public Policy in Emerging Economies
Volume/Issue: Vol. 4, No. 1 (2022)
DOI: 10.26710/rope.v4i1.2277

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: Taking the opening of the Kartarpur Corridor as a case study, this research paper highlights the divergent media perspectives across Indian and Pakistani newspapers published between 2020 and 2022. Applying Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA), the study reveals that Pakistani media predominantly framed the corridor as a symbol of peace, regional stability, religious tourism, and diplomatic breakthrough. In contrast, Indian media coverage focused heavily on security protocols, travel modalities, and interstate tensions. The research underscores the powerful role of media framing in shaping public perception, religious tourism, and peacebuilding initiatives between Pakistan and India.

publications.title: Human Capital the Key to Economic Growth: Some New Evidence from Selected Developing Countries
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: An empirical panel study investigating the impact of education and health human capital indicators on long-run economic growth across 43 developing countries using Pooled OLS estimation.

sections.title: Journal & Publication Details
sections.body:
Journal: Journal of Business and Social Review in Emerging Economies
Volume/Issue: Vol. 8, No. 1 (2022)
DOI: 10.26710/jbsee.v8i1.2135

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: Endogenous growth theory identifies human capital as the central driving force of long-term economic expansion. However, empirical literature on the specific roles of education versus health investments has yielded mixed conclusions. Utilizing a panel dataset of 43 developing countries spanning 1990 to 2018, this study estimates Pooled OLS models to evaluate how education and health indicators influence growth. The findings demonstrate that education proxies consistently drive long-run economic growth, while health expenditures become significantly positive when conditioned on education spending, urging policymakers to coordinate public health and education budgets.

publications.title: Most Stringent Test of Independence in W×K Contingency Tables for Nominal Data Using Monte Carlo Simulations
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: A statistical econometrics study using Monte Carlo simulations to establish that the Logarithmic Minimum Square (LMS) test is the most stringent test of independence in W x K contingency tables for nominal data.

sections.title: Journal & Publication Details
sections.body:
Journal: Sustainable Business and Society in Emerging Economies
Volume/Issue: Vol. 4, No. 1 (2022)
DOI: 10.26710/sbsee.v4i1.2145

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: Testing for independence in contingency tables is one of the most widely used statistical techniques in econometrics and empirical social science. However, researchers face ambiguity regarding the optimal test selection across different Data Generating Processes (DGPs) for nominal data. This study applies Stringent Criteria (SC) via Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate a wide range of independence tests in W × K contingency tables. The results demonstrate that the Logarithmic Minimum Square (LMS) test is optimal and superior to competing statistical tests, providing empirical econometricians with clear guidance for analyzing nominal contingency tables.

publications.title: The Role of Financial Inclusion in Income Inequality, Poverty Reduction & Economic Growth in Developing Countries
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: An econometric panel study of 101 developing countries utilizing System GMM estimation to analyze how expanding financial inclusion reduces income inequality and boosts economic growth.

sections.title: Journal & Publication Details
sections.body:
Journal: International Journal of Islamic Economics and Governance
Volume/Issue: Vol. 2, No. 2 (2021)
DOI: 10.58932/muld0006

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: This study examines the role of financial inclusion in driving economic growth, mitigating poverty, and lowering income inequality across 101 developing countries from 2010 to 2020. Data compiled from World Development Indicators and the World Bank Global Findex Database were analyzed using System Generalized Method of Moments (GMM). The empirical findings confirm that financial inclusion significantly boosts economic growth and narrows income inequality in developing nations. While financial inclusion operates indirectly on poverty alleviation through growth and distribution channels, policymakers are advised to expand access to formal financial services and digital banking infrastructure.

publications.title: Semi-Strong Form of Efficiency in South Asian Foreign Exchange Markets
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: An empirical evaluation of market efficiency across four South Asian foreign exchange markets (Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh) covering bilateral spot exchange rates from 1995 to 2015.

sections.title: Journal & Publication Details
sections.body:
Journal: IIIE Journal of Economics and Finance
Volume/Issue: Vol. 1, No. 2 (2020)
PDF Download: Download Full Paper

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: This study tests the weak-form and semi-strong form of market efficiency across four major South Asian foreign exchange markets: Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, and Bangladesh. Using monthly bilateral spot exchange rates against the US Dollar, British Pound, and Japanese Yen from January 1995 to December 2015, the empirical analysis confirms that all four markets conform to weak-form efficiency. However, the findings reject semi-strong form efficiency, demonstrating that regime shifts leave foreign exchange markets inefficient in the semi-strong sense and offering actionable insights for currency traders and macroeconomic regulators.

publications.title: Role of Remittance’s in Pakistan Economy; Analysis of the current status and guideline for Reforms
publications.author: أ.د. عطية ي. جافيد
publications.description: التقرير النهائي المقدم إلى لجنة التعليم العالي.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Reports/HEC final Report (Prof. Dr. Attiya Y. Javid - 21052020) (1)/Cover-image.png

sections.title: Executive Summary
sections.body:
Remittances for a very respectable size in the economy of Pakistan, and they form about 8.8% of GDP. These remittances play extremely important in management of Pakistan economy, mainly contributing to the management of current account balance. For a long period over the history, Pakistan is facing large trade deficit and the remittances are used to bring the current account deficit at balance. However, when remittances reach the country through formal channels, the bank keep the foreign currency with them and pay rupee in exchange of it. Thus about Rs. 3.3 trillion come into the pockets of recipients. The earlier studies on remittances show that the marginal propensity to save for the remitters is much higher compared to the overall propensity to save. Supposing marginal propensity to save to be only 20%, the amount of saving should be sufficient to finance millions of jobs. But no job related activities are observable.

The first question arises that how remittances contribute to the economy? A model was estimated using WALS approach which show that the huge surge in remittances didn’t effect the pace of growth of economy.

The second question that arises is; what is happening to the remittances that they don’t contribute to economy. Extensive Survey was carried out in selected cities of all four provinces, Azad Kashmir, Islamabad Capital territory and Gilgit Baltistan to find the answer to this question. The findings reveal that largest share of the investable part of remittances goes into real estate, especially sale and purchase of plots which is extremely capital intensive business and one doesn’t contribute to the employment generation and any other economic benefit.

The next important question was to recommend the measures for enhancing the flow of remittances through formal channels and to recommend measures for welfare of remittances. We propose that in order to increase the formal inflow, SBP should subsidize the formal inflow. This subsidy would be proportional to size of remittances and would not be directly encashable. Half of this subsidy is deposited to the premium for health and life insurance of the remitter and his/her family and remaining half of subsidy is to be deposited to a welfare fund for remitter. The amount deposited to the fund along with the profit would be payable to the remitter when he/she quits overseas job, or when he/she intends to finance the business of any of his heirs. Such a subsidy would be a goodwill gesture from the government for the remitters and would help remitters to start a business when he/she comes back to the homeland. Since this subsidy would not be directly encashable, it would not affect the current exchange rate.

The last and most important question was; how to utilize the remittances in better way. We have found from the data we collected that the major chunk of investable remittances goes into real estate and in particular, business of plots. This is extremely capital intensive business and we have to replace it with some labor intensive business. We argue that the investable part of remittances can be invested in the mega-development projects using bonds issued in the name of projects. The investors may be paid return when the project become mature. We argue that such an investment must be protected through proper legislation. We also discuss the necessary measures needed to make such investments viable.

publications.title: Test of Ownership Dispersion Theory as Explanation of Underpricing of New Issues in Pakistan
publications.author: Prof. Dr. Attiya Yasmin Javid, Malik Muhammad Shehryar, Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: An empirical investigation of 72 IPOs listed on the Karachi Stock Exchange (2000–2015) validating the ownership dispersion hypothesis as a primary explanation for initial public offering underpricing.

sections.title: Journal & Publication Details
sections.body:
Journal: Journal of Pakistan Economic Review, Quaid-e-Azam University, Islamabad
Date: January 2019
PDF Link: Download Full Paper

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: This paper tests the ownership dispersion hypothesis to explain the phenomenon of Initial Public Offering (IPO) underpricing using sample data of 72 IPOs issued at the Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) between 2000 and 2015. The hypothesis posits that firms deliberately underprice new issues to generate oversubscription and establish a broad shareholder base, thereby enhancing secondary market liquidity. Empirical results confirm that underpricing induces oversubscription and dispersed ownership, reducing risk for existing owners and establishing a liquid secondary trading market.

publications.title: The Effect of Various Relationship Factors on Business Success; Empirical Evidence from Business Partners of Pakistan and China
publications.author: Prof. Dr. Attiya Yasmin Javid, Shakeel Shahzad, Jawad Ali
publications.description: The existing study investigates the dynamic association among various dimensions of relationship and their impact on interpersonal and inter-organizational commitment...

sections.title: Abstract
sections.body: The existing study investigates the dynamic association among various dimensions of relationship and their impact on interpersonal and inter-organizational commitment in a sample of business partners from Pakistanis and Chinese companies that do business together in Pakistan. Path modeling was used to explore the hierarchical nature of the relationship dimensions amongst one another and on the dependent variables. We conclude that relationship variables in our cross-cultural study are hierarchical and that personal relationships are critical to building and enhancing inter-organizational relationships. We further noted that some relationship dimensions may not have significant direct relationships with commitment, but their indirect and total effects may be significant. Our results challenge conventional conceptualization of relationship dimensions by suggesting a hierarchy of importance among these dimensions.

publications.title: Blockchain in Public Governance: Can Technology Improve Transparency?
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Blockchain technology has the potential to improve public governance by making government records more transparent, traceable, and difficult to alter. It can support greater accountability in areas such as public procurement, financial management, social welfare, land registration, and regulatory compliance. However, blockchain alone cannot eliminate corruption or guarantee accurate information; its effectiveness depends on strong institutions, reliable data, privacy protection, legal frameworks, and independent oversight. Ultimately, blockchain can strengthen transparency and help citizens move from simply “trusting” government information to being able to “verify” it.

sections.title: Introduction: Moving Beyond Trust to Verification
sections.body:
Blockchain technology has moved far beyond its early association with cryptocurrencies. Today, governments, development organizations, and policymakers are exploring how blockchain can be used to improve public administration, strengthen accountability, and make government processes more transparent. At its core, blockchain offers a shared and tamper-resistant digital record that allows multiple parties to verify information without relying entirely on a single centralized database.

For governments, this creates a transformative opportunity: Can blockchain help citizens see how public resources are managed, how decisions are recorded, and where government processes may be vulnerable to manipulation?

"Technology alone cannot solve governance challenges, but it can strengthen the systems that uphold transparency and accountability."
TRANSPARENT GOVERNANCE | DATA INTEGRITY | PUBLIC TRUST

While the potential is significant, blockchain is not a magic solution. Its true value depends on the quality of data entered into the system, institutional capacity, robust legal frameworks, cybersecurity, and the genuine willingness of governments to make information publicly accessible and auditable.

sections.title: Potential Benefits of Blockchain in Public Governance
sections.body:
When applied thoughtfully in public governance, blockchain technology offers six key benefits that strengthen institutional integrity and citizen trust:

1. Enhanced Transparency

Open and verifiable digital records accessible to all stakeholders, reducing hidden transactions and information asymmetry.

2. Stronger Accountability

Immutable audit trails reduce opportunities for record tampering, unauthorized modifications, and administrative misuse.

3. Efficient Public Spending

Trace public funds from initial budget allocation down to project completion, ensuring spending aligns with legislative intent.

4. Trust & Confidence

Builds institutional trust between citizens and state bodies by replacing opaque procedures with verifiable data trails.

5. Data Integrity

Cryptographically secured, tamper-resistant records guarantee high data fidelity and protection against post-hoc manipulation.

6. Citizen Empowerment

Empowers citizens, oversight bodies, and journalists through direct access to transparent, auditable government data.

sections.title: Key Areas of Application
sections.body:
Blockchain can be deployed across several vital public sector domains to improve operational efficiency and public integrity:

1

Public Procurement

Recording tender announcements, bid submissions, evaluation milestones, contract awards, and modifications on an unalterable ledger prevents corruption and collusion.

2

Public Financial Management

Tracking government disbursements and infrastructure project funding ensures every rupee allocated reaches its intended expenditure line item.

3

Social Welfare Programs

Verifying direct transfers to targeted beneficiaries prevents ghost recipients, duplicate claims, and administrative leakages while safeguarding recipient privacy.

4

Land Registration & Property Rights

Creating chronological, immutable land ownership records reduces property disputes, protects titles, and facilitates secure economic investment.

5

Regulatory Compliance & Supply Chain

Monitoring cross-border trade, pharmaceutical supply chains, and environmental compliance records with cryptographic proof of authenticity.

sections.title: The Challenges Governments Must Consider
sections.body:
Despite its vast potential, implementing blockchain in public administration presents significant technical, legal, and operational hurdles:

Challenge AreaRisk / VulnerabilityStrategic Solution
1. Data Quality"Garbage in, garbage out": tamper-proof ledgers still preserve false initial data.Implement multi-party verification and pre-entry audit checks.
2. Privacy ProtectionPublic ledgers risking exposure of sensitive citizen identity & financial details.Deploy zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), encryption, and off-chain storage.
3. Infrastructure & CostHigh computational, storage, training, and transition costs for developing nations.Phase adoption starting with high-impact, targeted procurement systems.
4. InteroperabilityFragmented legacy databases unable to communicate with blockchain layers.Adopt open API standards and unified middleware architecture.
5. Legal FrameworksUnclear legal status of smart contracts, digital signatures, and cross-border data.Enact modernized digital evidence laws and statutory oversight rules.
6. Institutional ResistancePushback from centralized bureaucratic entities accustomed to opaque control.Combine technical deployment with strong political leadership & incentives.

sections.title: Blockchain Is Not a Replacement for Good Governance
sections.body:
One of the biggest misconceptions about blockchain is that technology alone can eradicate corruption. It cannot. Corruption is rooted in institutional weaknesses, poor incentives, weak enforcement, and political interference.

Blockchain reaches its maximum potential when integrated into a comprehensive digital governance stack:

Blockchain + Open Data + Digital Identity + Artificial Intelligence + Strong Institutions + Independent Auditing

Key Takeaway: The goal of digital transformation is to transition government from systems relying on "trust us" to transparent frameworks where citizens can independently "verify for themselves."

Strategic Policy Recommendations:
  • ✓ Begin with targeted pilot projects in high-risk areas like public procurement.
  • ✓ Ensure open-data dashboards translate complex blockchain ledgers into human-readable insights.
  • ✓ Establish robust data governance, privacy standards, and independent technical audit protocols.
  • ✓ Invest in digital skills and institutional capacity building across public sector agencies.

publications.title: Tax Incentives vs. Tax Revenue: When a Break Pays Off (and When It Doesn't)
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: This blog examines tax incentives versus tax revenue, focusing on when tax breaks can genuinely contribute to economic growth and when they simply reduce government revenue without creating additional benefits. It explains that effective incentives should address real investment barriers, influence decisions at the margin, be time-sensitive, generate positive spillovers such as jobs, training, productivity, and innovation, and include clear eligibility and enforcement mechanisms. The document also highlights common problems such as windfall gains, timing shifts, weak accountability, excessive competition between jurisdictions, and distributional trade-offs. It proposes evaluating incentives through incrementality, cost per outcome, fiscal feedback, opportunity cost, risk and enforceability, and spillovers, while recommending performance-based incentives, measurable targets, sunset clauses, and clawbacks.

sections.title: Introduction: Smart Incentives, Stronger Economy, Sustainable Future
sections.body:
Tax incentives can be a powerful tool to drive investment, innovation, and jobs—but only when they generate more value for the economy than the revenue they cost. The real question is not whether tax incentives are "good" or "bad"—it's whether they work.

Governments around the world, particularly in developing and emerging economies like Pakistan, frequently deploy tax breaks, credits, accelerated depreciation, and tax holidays to attract capital and stimulate business activity. However, when poorly designed, tax incentives can severely erode the national tax base without delivering tangible economic returns.

"Tax incentives should be treated as investments: they should be targeted, transparent, performance-based, and continued only when their broader economic benefits justify the revenue forgone."
SMART INCENTIVES | STRONGER ECONOMY | SUSTAINABLE FUTURE

sections.title: The Case for Tax Incentives: Correcting Frictions & Unlocking Capital
sections.body:
At their best, tax incentives correct real economic frictions and unlock strategic investments that create broad societal value:

1. Reducing Risk & Capital Cost

Credits and accelerated depreciation lower upfront capital costs and assist in financing major long-term infrastructure and industrial projects.

2. Capturing Positive Spillovers

Investments in R&D, workforce training, and industrial clusters generate broad societal gains that the private investor cannot fully monetize alone.

3. Competing for Mobile Activity

In a globally competitive marketplace, targeted incentives help attract mobile foreign investment, regional corporate HQs, tech hubs, and high-skilled jobs.

4. Targeting Hard-to-Start Markets

Incentives unlock critical capital for underserved sectors such as affordable housing, renewable clean energy, and brownfield redevelopment.

sections.title: When Incentives Truly Work: The 5 Core Principles
sections.body:
Real impact occurs when incentives are targeted, time-sensitive, and strictly tied to verifiable results:

1

Project is on the Margin (Incrementality)

Incentives must alter the decision—between locations, scale, or timing—turning a project "no" into a definite "yes".

2

Front-Loaded Benefits

Upfront incentives (investment tax credits, immediate expensing) influence decisions far more effectively than distant future tax breaks.

3

Positive Economic Spillovers

Job creation is key, but wider benefits like domestic supplier integration, tech diffusion, skills training, and productivity growth matter even more.

4

Clear Rules & Strict Enforcement

Transparent eligibility rules, mandatory reporting, sunset clauses, and clawback provisions prevent gaming and protect fiscal resources.

5

Economy Can Absorb Growth

Robust physical infrastructure, skilled labor, housing, and fast regulatory permitting ensure incentives spark genuine economic output rather than price inflation.

sections.title: Investment-Driven Impact vs. Windfall Profits: A Comparative Analysis
sections.body:
To understand the difference between effective incentives and wasteful revenue drain, consider two simplified scenarios:

FeatureExample A: Investment-Driven ImpactExample B: Windfall for Existing Profits
Incentive Structure10% investment credit on a new $400M industrial plant.Blanket corporate tax reduction for an already profitable firm.
Behavioral ShiftBridges financing cost gap, attracts supply chain partners, funds college training.Saves money for firm without changing business plans or investment scope.
Economic ResultProject moves from "No" to "Yes". High jobs + spillovers = Net Economic Gain.Lost government revenue with zero additional economic activity generated.

sections.title: Policy Framework & Key Takeaways for Fiscal Governance
sections.body:
Tax incentives should be systematically evaluated against six criteria: incrementality, cost per outcome, fiscal feedback loops, opportunity costs, risk and enforceability, and broader spillovers.

Key Takeaway: Good incentives are targeted, time-bound, performance-linked, and transparent. Bad incentives are broad, permanent, and opaque—they drain government revenue without delivering results.

Strategic Policy Actions:
  • ✓ Shift from discretionary tax holidays to performance-based tax credits.
  • ✓ Enforce mandatory sunset clauses and clawback provisions for non-compliance.
  • ✓ Conduct annual public cost-benefit audits of all active tax incentive schemes.
  • ✓ Design tax incentives that reward performance, not privilege—building a stronger Pakistan.

publications.title: Why Cashless Economies Are Growing – And What It Means for Consumers
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: Cashless economies are growing as digital payments, smartphones, e-commerce, fintech, and modern payment systems make transactions faster and more convenient. While cashless payments can improve financial efficiency, financial inclusion, spending management, and access to financial services, they also create challenges such as privacy concerns, cybersecurity risks, financial exclusion, and dependence on technology. The future is likely to be a less-cash economy, where digital payments become dominant while cash remains available for people who need it.

sections.title: Introduction: The Shift Toward a Digital Financial Ecosystem
sections.body:
Cashless economies are reshaping the way we pay, live, and connect. As digital payment platforms become the new global normal, they offer unprecedented convenience, economic opportunities—and new societal responsibilities.

Across emerging markets, including Pakistan, financial ecosystems are rapidly evolving beyond paper currency toward digital wallets, instant micro-payments, QR codes, and online banking. While the shift holds immense potential for expanding financial access and efficiency, managing the transition requires balancing rapid innovation with financial protection.

"The future is digital, but inclusive. A smart cashless economy ensures choice, security, and financial inclusion for all."
BUILDING A FINANCIAL FUTURE THAT WORKS FOR EVERYONE

sections.title: What's Driving the Shift Toward Cashless Transactions?
sections.body:
Five key pillars are accelerating the global adoption of cashless and digital payment channels:

1. Technology Innovation

Smartphones, user-friendly fintech applications, biometric authentication, and high-speed mobile internet enable instant payments anywhere.

2. E-Commerce Boom

The rapid expansion of online shopping, ride-hailing, food delivery, and digital service platforms necessitates seamless digital payment rails.

3. Post-Pandemic Behavioral Shift

COVID-19 permanently accelerated consumer preferences for contactless transactions, digital wallets, and hygienic payment methods.

4. Government & Policy Support

State initiatives, modern central bank payment gateways (like Raast in Pakistan), and supportive regulatory frameworks lower digital transaction costs.

5. Evolving Consumer Expectations

Modern consumers demand speed, simplicity, 24/7 availability, and frictionless transactions across all retail and service touchpoints.

sections.title: Benefits for Consumers vs. Challenges to Consider
sections.body:
The transition to digital transactions offers substantial advantages, but also introduces critical vulnerabilities that policy-makers and consumers must navigate:

Key Benefits for ConsumersChallenges & Vulnerabilities
Convenience & Speed: Pay anytime, anywhere without carrying cash. Privacy & Data Security: Risks of unauthorized data tracking and personal exposure.
Financial Tracking & Budgeting: Automatic digital receipts allow accurate expense monitoring. Digital Divide & Exclusion: Vulnerable or unbanked populations may be left behind without cash options.
Access to Credit & Services: Digital history builds creditworthiness for micro-loans and investments. Cybersecurity Threats: Phishing, ransomware, account takeovers, and digital payment fraud risks.
Physical Safety: Eliminates loss or theft associated with carrying large cash sums. Technology Dependence: System outages or lack of internet grid connection can halt payments.

sections.title: The Future Is Digital, But Inclusive: The 5 Strategic Pillars
sections.body:
The ultimate goal for developing economies is not a zero-cash society, but a "less-cash" ecosystem where digital transactions dominate while cash remains accessible for those who need it.

1. SECURE

Robust cybersecurity infrastructure and consumer protection build public trust.

2. INCLUSIVE

Ensuring low-income, rural, and elderly populations retain equal financial access.

3. INNOVATIVE

Supporting fintech growth, open banking, and instant interoperable payment rails.

4. SUSTAINABLE

Building digital financial architecture that supports long-term economic resilience.

5. CONNECTED

Seamlessly linking merchants, banks, consumers, and government services.

sections.title: Conclusion: Balancing Innovation with Financial Resilience
sections.body:
A cashless transition succeeds only when technology empowers consumers rather than excluding them. By combining state-of-the-art payment infrastructure with digital literacy and strong regulatory safeguards, countries can build an economic future that is efficient, secure, and truly inclusive.

Strategic Imperatives:
  • ✓ Strengthen cyber resilience and data privacy protection laws.
  • ✓ Promote financial literacy and digital onboarding for underserved communities.
  • ✓ Maintain cash infrastructure as a reliable fallback for emergency resilience.
  • ✓ Foster public-private partnerships to lower merchant transaction fees.

publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: The world is moving toward a technology-driven future, with Artificial Intelligence, quantum computing, autonomous vehicles, smart cities, biotechnology, renewable energy, robotics, brain-computer interfaces, 3D printing, and space technology expected to reshape industries by 2030. These innovations can improve productivity, healthcare, transportation, energy efficiency, manufacturing, and human connectivity while creating new economic opportunities. However, realizing their benefits will require investment in digital infrastructure, skills, research, cybersecurity, responsible governance, and ethical development.
publications.thumbnail: /assets/data/Publications/Blogs/10 Future Technologies That Will Change the World by 2030/FRPD-EI-2026-773-30_Banner.jpg

sections.title: Introduction: Navigating the Technological Frontier of 2030
sections.body:
The period leading to 2030 could represent one of the most significant technological transformations in modern history. The world is moving toward a technology-driven future where emerging innovations move out of research labs and into mainstream economic, industrial, and social life.

Ten key technological domains—Artificial Intelligence, quantum computing, autonomous vehicles, smart cities, biotechnology, renewable energy, robotics, brain-computer interfaces, 3D printing, and space technology—are expected to reshape industries and societies over the coming decade.

"Innovation today shapes a smarter, faster, greener, and more inclusive world for tomorrow."
SMARTER | FASTER | GREENER | BETTER FUTURE

These innovations promise to improve productivity, healthcare, transportation, energy efficiency, manufacturing, and human connectivity while creating new economic opportunities. However, realizing their full benefits requires investment in digital infrastructure, human skills, research, cybersecurity, responsible governance, and ethical development.

sections.title: The 10 Frontier Technologies Reshaping the World
sections.body:
Each of the ten technologies represents a distinct pillar of the emerging global digital economy:

1. Artificial Intelligence (AI)

AI systems process vast datasets, automate complex tasks, and support decision-making across healthcare, agriculture, finance, manufacturing, and knowledge work while demanding safety, transparency, and ethical governance.

2. Quantum Computing

Leveraging quantum-mechanical principles, quantum computers solve complex problems beyond classical systems—revolutionizing drug discovery, materials science, optimization, and post-quantum cybersecurity encryption.

3. Autonomous Vehicles

Self-driving cars and intelligent transport networks combine sensors, cameras, and AI to improve road safety, reduce traffic congestion, expand accessibility, and automate urban logistics.

4. Smart Cities

Connected IoT infrastructure, real-time data platforms, and intelligent traffic/energy networks create efficient, sustainable, and people-friendly urban services.

5. Biotechnology Advancements

Gene editing, personalized medicine, and bio-innovations improve disease treatment, extend healthy life expectancy, and support climate-resilient agriculture.

6. Renewable Energy Tech

Solar, wind, next-generation batteries, and smart grids power a cleaner, decentralized, and energy-secure future while driving down industrial costs.

7. Robotics & Automation

Advanced robotics handles complex, dangerous, and repetitive tasks in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare, boosting productivity while reshaping labor skill needs.

8. Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs)

Direct communication between neural pathways and digital devices unlocks breakthrough medical therapies, assistive devices, and direct human-machine interactions.

9. 3D Printing Evolution

Additive manufacturing enables rapid prototyping, custom medical devices, complex aerospace components, and decentralized localized manufacturing.

10. Space Technology

Satellite constellations, Earth observation, lunar missions, and commercial space exploration open new frontiers for disaster response, agriculture, and global communications.

sections.title: The Power of Technological Convergence
sections.body:
The defining feature of the 2030 landscape is not merely the growth of individual technologies, but their powerful convergence:

Convergence AreaIntegrated TechnologiesImpact Outcome
Intelligent AutomationAI + Robotics + 3D PrintingFully automated, customizable factories with zero-latency quality control.
Sustainable Urban MobilityAutonomous Vehicles + Smart Cities + Renewable EnergyZero-emission self-driving urban transit networks synced to smart grid demand.
Precision Health & Bio-AIBiotechnology + AI + BCIsReal-time health monitoring, neural interfaces, and AI-designed gene therapies.
Resilient Global InfrastructureSpace Tech + IoT + Quantum ComputingSatellite climate tracking, unhackable quantum encryption, and global coverage.

sections.title: Preparing for the Technological Future: Policy & Strategic Priorities
sections.body:
Technological progress alone does not guarantee social or economic progress. Countries and organizations require coordinated frameworks to capture benefits while managing risks:

1

Digital Infrastructure & Connectivity

Expand high-speed broadband, secure cloud data centers, IoT sensor networks, and satellite access to bridge digital divides and foster universal participation.

2

Human Capital & Workforce Skilling

Realign curricula around STEM, programming, data literacy, critical thinking, and lifelong learning to prepare workers for automated and AI-augmented roles.

3

Cybersecurity & Responsible Governance

Implement transparent AI guidelines, strict data privacy standards, post-quantum encryption, and ethical guardrails across genetic, biological, and neural data.

4

R&D Investment & Enterprise Transformation

Incentivize private and public sector research, support startup ecosystems, and accelerate digital adoption to ensure long-term industrial competitiveness.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Future Belongs to Proactive Leaders
sections.body:
The central question facing leaders today is no longer whether technology will transform the global economy, but how effectively societies will manage and direct that transformation.

Core Takeaway: "The future is coming. Be ready. Technological progress must be accompanied by responsible governance, investment in human capital, cybersecurity, ethical standards, and equal access to opportunities."

Strategic Imperatives:
  • ✓ Build robust digital infrastructure and clean energy systems.
  • ✓ Invest continuously in human talent, STEM skills, and digital literacy.
  • ✓ Establish clear ethical, privacy, and cybersecurity guardrails.
  • ✓ Harness technology convergence to drive sustainable, inclusive economic growth.

publications.title: From Chatbots to AI Agents: The Next Revolution in Business
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: The blog explains how artificial intelligence is evolving from traditional chatbots that simply answer questions into AI agents capable of planning, making decisions, using business tools, maintaining context, and completing entire workflows. AI agents can create significant value across customer service, sales, finance, HR, and IT by reducing processing time, improving quality, increasing efficiency, and supporting better decision-making. However, their greater autonomy also introduces risks related to accuracy, data privacy, security, compliance, access, and accountability. The document recommends a responsible approach that begins with measurable use cases, clean data, controlled permissions, strong guardrails, human oversight, continuous measurement, and gradual scaling.

sections.title: Introduction: The Shift from Answering Questions to Completing Outcomes
sections.body:
If you think AI in your business starts and ends with a chatbot answering FAQs, you’re already behind. The next wave isn’t about better conversation—it’s about systems that can plan, decide, and act across workflows with minimal human prompting.

Chatbots are primarily conversational. They take a prompt, retrieve information, and generate a plausible response. At their best, they function like a smart interface on top of a knowledge base—useful, but fundamentally reactive.

AI agents change the center of gravity. An agent is designed to achieve a goal (for example: "resolve this customer issue," "reconcile these invoices," or "launch a campaign") by sequencing tasks over time. Instead of replying once, it can break work into steps, call tools, check results, and continue until it reaches an outcome—or hands off when uncertainty is high.

"The unit of automation is expanding from a single task to an end-to-end workflow."
Leaders who adapt early will lead the next decade.

This shift matters because business value rarely comes from a single response. It comes from reducing cycle time, eliminating rework, improving compliance, and increasing throughput. Agents are a better match for that reality because they operate across processes, not just conversations.

sections.title: What Makes AI Agents More Capable (and More Disruptive)
sections.body:
AI agents aren’t magic; they’re an architectural step forward. Several capabilities combine to make them meaningfully more powerful than chatbots in business environments:

Planning & Decomposition

Translate high-level goals into multi-step execution plans, prioritize sub-tasks, and adapt dynamically as new information appears.

Tool Use & Integration

Connect with enterprise APIs and software (CRM, ERP, databases, ticketing systems) to retrieve live data and take concrete operational actions.

Memory & Context Management

Maintain short-term and persistent context across steps and sessions, enabling workflow continuity without repetitive handoffs.

Feedback Loops & Self-Checks

Validate outputs against constraints, verify numerical calculations, check organizational policies, and ensure quality before execution.

Orchestration & Multi-Agent Systems

Multiple specialized agents collaborate across domains (research, drafting, compliance review, execution), with coordinator agents managing workflows and escalation paths.

sections.title: Where AI Agents Create Business Value (Beyond Productivity Hype)
sections.body:
The strongest use cases share three traits: they’re process-heavy, they involve high context, and they benefit from consistent execution. Agents can reduce time-to-resolution, increase capacity without linear headcount growth, and improve quality by embedding best practices directly into the workflow.

FunctionHigh-Value Agent OutcomesWhat to Measure
Customer Operations
Triages tickets, gathers account context, proposes resolutions, drafts responses, triggers refunds/credits within policy, escalates edge cases.Time to first response, time to resolution, escalation rate, CSAT, policy exceptions.
Sales
Builds account briefs, logs CRM updates, drafts follow-ups, schedules meetings, recommends next best actions based on pipeline signals.Rep admin time saved, meeting-to-opportunity conversion, CRM data completeness, sales cycle time.
Finance
Extracts invoice data, matches PO/receipts, flags anomalies, prepares close checklists, drafts variance narratives.Days-to-close, exception rate, audit adjustments, cost per invoice.
HR & People Ops
Answers policy questions, drafts role descriptions, coordinates onboarding steps, generates manager guides, routes approvals.Time-to-onboard, ticket volume, manager satisfaction, policy adherence.
IT & Security Operations
Classifies incidents, gathers logs, runs playbooks, creates change tickets, recommends remediation with approvals.MTTR, false positives, change failure rate, % automated playbook steps.

Practical Takeaway: Start where work is already standardized and measurable. Agents earn trust fastest when they deliver clear operational KPIs—not vague "innovation."

sections.title: Risks Leaders Must Manage: Governance Is Non-Negotiable
sections.body:
Agents introduce a new category of risk because they don’t just say things—they can do things. That creates exposure across brand, financial controls, privacy, and regulatory compliance if guardrails are weak or responsibilities are unclear.

Accuracy & Hallucinations

Confident but wrong outputs can translate directly into operational errors (incorrect refunds, flawed reporting, bad configs). Fact-checking, automated validation, and confidence thresholds are essential.

Data Privacy & Security

Protect sensitive business and customer data. Tool access must strictly follow least-privilege principles, with explicit technical guardrails against prompt leakage and unauthorized data exposure.

Compliance & Auditability

Log all agent actions and decisions for end-to-end auditability. Ensure automation cannot bypass internal financial controls, approval hierarchies, or segregation of duties.

Human Oversight & Accountability

Keep humans in the loop for high-impact decisions. Clear ownership must be established upfront across business owners, IT, and operations rather than deferring blame to "the model."

sections.title: How to Get Started: A Responsible 5-Step Journey
sections.body:
Winning with AI agents is less about choosing a vendor and more about building operating discipline: clear outcomes, clean data paths, controlled tool access, and continuous measurement. The goal is not maximum autonomy on day one—it’s repeatable, governed value.

1

Choose the Right Use Case

Start with standardized, measurable, high-volume processes with clearly defined inputs and outputs (ticket resolution, invoice matching, employee onboarding). Define baseline KPIs upfront.

2

Prepare Your Data & Tools

Ensure high data quality, secure access boundaries, and reliable API integrations. Implement least privilege access, approval gates, and audit logging from day one.

3

Design the Workflow & Guardrails

Define clear success criteria, exception handling rules, and human escalation triggers. Ensure that admitting uncertainty is a standard, safe fallback for the agent.

4

Pilot, Measure, & Improve

Run a staged rollout: begin in Observe mode (recommendations only), progress to Assist mode (human-in-the-loop validation), and iterate based on real error logs and user satisfaction metrics.

5

Scale Responsibly

Expand autonomy only for low-risk actions while hardening governance, monitoring model drift, versioning system prompts and tools, and standardizing documentation across teams.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Competitive Advantage Goes to the Best Operators
sections.body:
Chatbots made information easier to access. AI agents will make execution faster, cheaper, and more consistent, especially for organizations that treat them like a strategic capability with governance, metrics, and clear accountability.

Your next step: identify one high-friction workflow, define success metrics, and pilot an agent with strict permissions and human oversight. The companies that start building this responsibly now won’t just "use AI"—they’ll redesign how work gets done.

Strategic Takeaways:
  • ✓ AI agents don't just answer questions—they get work done.
  • ✓ Deploy thoughtfully. Govern rigorously. Scale confidently.
  • ✓ The future belongs to organizations that build intelligent, trustworthy systems today.

publications.title: Pakistan's Economic Outlook for FY 2026-2027: From Crisis Management to Sustainable Growth
publications.author: Dr. Shakeel Shahzad
publications.description: In this blog we examine Pakistan’s transition from economic stabilization toward sustainable, productivity-driven growth. It highlights recent improvements in GDP growth, foreign-exchange reserves, inflation management, fiscal performance, and international confidence, while emphasizing that stabilization alone cannot resolve Pakistan’s long-standing structural challenges. The report identifies key priorities including broadening the tax base, reforming the energy sector, diversifying and increasing exports, attracting productive private investment, expanding the digital economy and AI sector, reforming state-owned enterprises, strengthening human capital, and integrating climate resilience into economic planning. Overall, it argues that Pakistan must move away from repeated cycles of crisis, borrowing, and temporary stabilization toward an economy based on productivity, investment, exports, technological innovation, human capital, and sustainable growth.

sections.title: Introduction: From Macroeconomic Stability to Long-Term Economic Transformation
sections.body:
For much of the past decade, Pakistan’s economic narrative has been dominated by recurring balance-of-payments pressures, double-digit inflation, currency depreciation, rising public debt, energy-sector bottlenecks, and recurring negotiations with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Each episode followed an unsustainable cycle: foreign-exchange reserves fell, import financing froze, the currency slumped, and emergency stabilization measures became unavoidable.

Today, Pakistan stands at a crucial economic crossroads. Immediate default risks have receded, macroeconomic indicators have stabilized, and fiscal and external buffers are being rebuilt. The Pakistan Economic Survey 2025–26 provisionally estimates real GDP growth at 3.7% in FY2026, up from 3.18% in FY2025. Agriculture, industrial activity, and services have all contributed to this recovery.

"Stabilization prevents a crisis. Transformation prevents the next one."
Evidence. Efficiency. Impact. Navigating Pakistan's transition from crisis management to sustainable growth.

However, stabilization must not be mistaken for structural transformation. The central question is no longer merely "How do we avoid the next crisis?" but "How do we build an economy that does not repeatedly produce the same crises?"

sections.title: The Stabilization Phase: Progress, but Not the Finish Line
sections.body:
Pakistan’s macroeconomic stabilization has been anchored by disciplined monetary policies and the IMF’s Extended Fund Facility (EFF) and Resilience and Sustainability Facility (RSF). In May 2026, the IMF completed its third review under the EFF and second review under the RSF, enabling total disbursements under both programs to reach approximately US$4.8 billion.
